source_read: PDF, pp. 154–160 (all 7 pages read; Table 1 and Figure 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; online supplementary table and funnel plot not available in the PDF and not read)

claims.overstatement: As far as this source goes, 'largest for learning and memory' is not supported. In Potvin et al. the largest pooled differences were impulsivity/reward tasks (d 0.93, 8 studies) and social cognition (d 1.12, 3 studies). Among conventional domains verbal learning was largest (0.59), but verbal memory (0.40) and visual memory (0.47) were in the common range and visual learning (0.28) was not significant. The magnitude line '44 studies, 1592 vs 1820: global d 0.46' should say the global estimate pools 27 of the 44 studies; participant numbers for those 27 are not given.
claims.note: Checked against Table 1 (p. 157): global d 0.462 (95% CI 0.329–0.595), 27 studies, random effects, Q=53.4 (my I² ≈51%); positive d = users worse (p. 156), so 'in favour of controls' is right. 9 of 12 domains lie between 0.28 and 0.59, consistent with 'about 0.3 to 0.7 SD for most domains'. Publication bias: Egger t=5.1, p=0.00003 (p. 156); the authors give no bias-adjusted estimate. Early abstinence: weighted mean 4.5 months (3.3 months without one long-abstinence study) in the 14 of 27 studies that reported it (p. 158). This source gives no information on education differences between users and controls (only a meta-regression on users' mean education), so the education sentence must rest on other sources. The inclusion criteria did not require abstinence, and at least one included study tested current users (Simon et al., 2002, by its title in the reference list, p. 160).

anchors.extracted: 44 studies included, 1592 people with a methamphetamine use disorder and 1820 healthy controls; 124 full texts assessed, 80 excluded (25 no control group, 13 missing data, 13 HIV, 16 duplicate samples, 5 not meeting DSM-IV criteria, 8 tasks in fMRI).
Largest: impulsivity 0.926 (0.716–1.135), 8 studies; social cognition 1.117 (0.810–1.423), 3 studies, both fixed-effect. Visual learning 0.275 (−0.107 to 0.657), 5 studies, p=0.158.
Egger's regression on the global measure: t=5.1, p=0.00003; funnel plot only in the online supplement.

anchors.locator: Discussion, paragraph on length of abstinence (right column)
anchors.extracted: Only 14 of 27 studies gave abstinence data; weighted mean 4.5 months, 3.3 months after excluding McCann et al. (2008; mean 77.4 months); most studies had short abstinence.

Tests averaged within study per domain; fixed or random effects chosen by Q test at p<0.1; results more than 2 SD from the composite excluded as outliers (applied to speed of processing and visuospatial, Table 1 footnotes).

claims.note: This source supports the cross-sectional part only: length of abstinence did not moderate the global difference, and almost all studies tested early abstinence. The printed 95% CI for the abstinence slope (−0.17 to 0.01 around β −0.004) is not consistent with the point estimate (probably −0.017); the other three meta-regression intervals are symmetric.

anchors.extracted: Meta-regression on global effect size: length of abstinence, 14 studies, β=−0.004 (95% CI printed −0.17 to 0.01), p=0.61; age, sex ratio and education also non-significant; α divided by the number of meta-regressions (p. 156, Methods 2.3).

anchors.locator: Discussion, paragraph on length of abstinence
anchors.extracted: No negative association between abstinence and deficits; authors attribute this to little variation between studies (one study at 77.4 months; weighted mean 3.3 months without it) and say the abstinence periods may have been too short to show an effect.

claims.note: The source supports 'not established' and 'no study measured cognition before use began'. It does not itself document education differences between groups. The authors lean the other way in one place: they read the null education meta-regression as tentatively suggesting the deficits are secondary to use, and the Results call them deficits 'induced by' use (p. 156). This is an interpretation the design cannot support, so it does not weaken the claim.

anchors.extracted: Authors state it is impossible to determine whether reward/impulse dysfunctions are caused by chronic use or precede it; impulsivity traits predict progression to misuse and impulsive disorders are common in the population studied.

anchors.locator: Discussion, paragraph on premorbid impairment (right column)
anchors.extracted: Premorbid impairment is acknowledged as a limitation of the field; no premorbid data were available; education used as a proxy; firm conclusions require longitudinal studies measuring premorbid functioning.

Effects of amount and duration of use, route, depressive symptoms, alcohol and smoking could not be examined; abstinence missing in 13 of 27 studies; publication bias means deficits are probably over-estimated.

key_findings.correction: Add: social cognition's Q=4.7 with 2 df gives p≈0.095, below the paper's own p<0.1 heterogeneity rule, yet it was pooled with fixed effects (no footnote a in Table 1).

reporting_issues.note: The age, sex and education intervals are symmetric around their estimates; only the abstinence interval is not.
Text on p. 156 (Results 3.1); Figure 1 on p. 157.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. Add: the highlights, abstract and discussion describe visuospatial ability as relatively spared and psychostimulants as unlikely to impair it (pp. 154, 158), while Table 1 shows d 0.39 (0.13–0.65, p=0.004), about the same as language (0.43) and verbal memory (0.40).

missed: Reporting issue: social cognition (Q=4.7, df=2, p≈0.095) meets the paper's own criterion for heterogeneity (p<0.1) but was pooled with a fixed-effect model, which narrows its interval (Table 1, p. 157; rule on p. 156).

The global estimate (d 0.46) pools 27 of the 44 studies (those with two or more domains); the number of participants behind it is not reported. The encyclopedia's magnitude line pairs it with '44 studies, 1592 vs 1820'.

The domain profile does not support 'largest for learning and memory' as a general statement: the largest effects here are impulsivity/reward and social cognition (Table 1). The card's 'where it stands' already notes the domain profile differs between meta-analyses.
Abstinence was not an inclusion criterion; at least one included study is of current users (Simon et al., 2002, per its title, p. 160), so the pooled estimates mix current and abstinent users.
Potvin et al. describe Scott et al. (2007) as 18 studies with 487 users and 464 controls (p. 155); see my scott_2007 file for what Scott reports.
